q: Which signal lets a program clean up before it exits: SIGTERM or SIGKILL?
expl: SIGTERM can be caught, so the program can save and tidy up. SIGKILL stops it instantly.
ch: Stop it politely: kill sends SIGTERM
opts: SIGTERM (plain kill)
SIGKILL (kill -9)
Both do

q: Which command lists processes with the highest CPU use first?
expl: The minus sign sorts from highest to lowest. Plain ps aux is sorted by process ID.
opts: ps aux | head
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head
pgrep -a cpu

q: Type a command that finds the processes whose name contains `busy` and prints each PID with its full command line.
expl: `pgrep -a` prints the PID and the whole command line; plain `pgrep` prints only the numbers.

q: Processes named `busy` and `busylog` are running. What does `-x` change in `pgrep -x busy`?
expl: `-x` asks for an exact name match, so similar names don't match by accident.
opts: It also prints the command line
Only the process named exactly `busy` matches, not `busylog`
It kills the process after finding it

q: Processes named `busy` and `busylog` are running. Type a command that stops only `busy`, with the default signal (SIGTERM).
expl: Plain `kill` and `pkill` send SIGTERM. `-x` keeps `pkill` from also hitting `busylog`.
ch: Stop it politely: kill sends SIGTERM

q: `worker.sh` traps SIGTERM: it prints "cleaning up" and removes its lock file. It is running now. What does this print?
expl: `pkill` sends SIGTERM, the trap runs, and the worker tidies up before it exits.
ch: Stop it politely: kill sends SIGTERM
opts: cleaning up\nlock file removed
lock file removed
/tmp/worker.lock
show: pkill -f worker.sh; sleep 1.5; cat worker.log; ls /tmp/worker.lock 2>/dev/null || echo "lock file removed"

q: You stop the same worker with `kill -9` instead. What happens to its lock file `/tmp/worker.lock`?
expl: The kernel removes the process instantly. Use `-9` only for a process that ignores plain `kill`.
ch: Why kill -9 is the last resort
opts: It's removed, just like with plain `kill`
It stays behind: SIGKILL can't be caught, so the cleanup never runs
`kill -9` refuses to stop a process that traps signals

q: Why use `top -b -n 1` in a script or a log?
expl: `-b` is batch mode (plain text), and `-n 1` stops after one update.
opts: It sorts the list by memory
It prints one snapshot and exits, instead of taking over the screen
It shows only the single busiest process

q: Which command lists the processes using the most memory first?
expl: RSS is the memory really in use, and the minus sign sorts from highest to lowest.
opts: `ps -eo pid,rss,comm --sort=rss | head`
`ps -eo pid,rss,comm --sort=-rss | head`
`ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head`
